name: Zane Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say gets your name attached. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a bulk feed lorry for the feed mill outside the village. It's a blower, so I pull up at a farm, hook a pipe to the bin and blow ten tonnes of pig or cattle feed up into it. Five or six farms a day, narrow lanes, mud, gates you've got to get out and open. I know most of the farmers, and half of them are my dad's age and have known me since I was a boy.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Hannah, my fiancée, in a rented cottage at the end of Church Lane. We're getting married next June at St Michael's, so every spare penny is going on that, and we've got maybe three weeks of money if something went wrong. I don't use AI and I don't want to. My dad's a mechanic and he says if you can't fix it with a spanner, don't buy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, it was a lot of hot air from people in cities. Farmers will always need feeding their animals, and someone's got to back a lorry down a lane. I'd say it at the pub, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's not that simple, though. The mill got bought by a big national group last year and they're cutting costs everywhere. They've already stopped the Saturday runs and talk about merging routes with the depot two counties over. AI or no AI, I'm worried about my hours, with the wedding coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do every run well, so they've got no reason to cut me. Hannah and I would trim the wedding a bit, maybe fewer guests. I'd ask my dad if I can do a few Saturdays at his garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, honestly. Not about robots, about the mill and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides the routes now, since the takeover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some office in the city with a computer. They don't know that the Hendersons' lane floods in February, or that you can't get round the back of Brook Farm with a full load. I end up phoning the farmers myself to sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trimming the wedding look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer guests, maybe ninety instead of a hundred and twenty. Hannah's mum would be upset. But I'd rather start married life without a loan.

say: I'd say the AI talk was **hot air** from people in cities.
I'd say farmers always need a lorry down the **lane**.
think: The mill's **new owners** are cutting costs and merging routes.
I'm worried about my **hours** with the wedding next June.
do: Do every run well so there's **no reason** to cut him.
Cut the **wedding** guest list from one hundred and twenty to ninety.
Pick up **Saturday work** at his dad's garage.
feel: **Worried** about the mill and money, not about robots.
S0.quote: AI or no AI, I'm worried about my hours, with the wedding coming.
fieldNote: Zane's pressure comes from the **takeover** of the feed mill by a national group.
He distrusts **distant office** planners who don't know local lanes.
He prefers **family work** over any outside help.

steps.text: Cut the wedding guest list from one hundred and twenty to ninety
Work Saturdays at his dad's garage for extra money
Keep the feed runs spotless so the mill has no reason to cut him

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the city lot are in trouble, not us. You can't blow feed into a bin from a laptop. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the office that would use AI to plan routes, and they'd cut a lorry. They already think one driver can do my run and someone else's, if the software says so. With the new owners, I'd be expecting a letter. There's one other feed firm near here and they're not hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the farmers I deliver to if they need help, in case I need work. I'd keep doing Saturdays at Dad's garage. I'd learn the delivery tablet if they bring one in, but only what I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit bitter. It feels like the people in offices make decisions and we pay for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a union or a group of drivers to push back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's not me. I'd rather sort it myself and with my family. My granddad always said a man stands on his own two feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we might have to tighten belts, but we'll manage. Her dad's got some land and a few cattle, and he's said there's always work there. I'd rather not, but family's family.

say: I'd say the **city** jobs are in trouble, not the drivers.
I'd say you can't blow feed from a **laptop**.
think: The office uses AI to **plan routes** and cut a lorry.
With the **new owners**, I'd expect a letter, and there are few other feed firms.
do: Ask local **farmers** if they need help.
feel: **Anxious** and **bitter** that office people decide while drivers pay.
S1.quote: You can't blow feed into a bin from a laptop.
fieldNote: Zane sees the **office side** changing first and driving jobs cut as a result.
He rejects **unions** and prefers standing on his own feet.
Family offers work on **Hannah's father's** land as a fallback.

steps.text: Ask the farmers on his feed round about farm work
Keep working Saturdays at his dad's garage
Learn just enough of the mill's delivery tablet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when you let big tech run the country. I'd say it at the pub and in church, where people are already worried. Not online, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the office side would be gone in 2028 and the robots would come for the lorry around 2031. Farm deliveries are messy, so maybe I'd last a bit longer, but not much. I've got no savings, no other skills except a bit of garage work. Hannah and I would be married with nothing coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Hannah's dad and ask about working on the farm full-time. I'd push the wedding back a year to save the money. Beyond that, I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like the ground's going from under us just as we're starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want the wedding at St Michael's, even with that hanging over you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's the one thing I wouldn't give up. It might be smaller and later, but the vows matter more than the party.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years after the AGI. Does that gap help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a bit. Three years of driving while I figure out what's next. But the people who plan and pay me would already be machines, so I'd be on borrowed time.

say: I'd blame **big tech** running the country.
I'd say it at the **pub** and in **church**, not online.
think: The office goes in 2028 and the **lorry** around **2031**.
Married with **nothing coming in** is what I'd fear most.
do: Ask **Hannah's dad** about full-time work on his cattle farm.
Push the **wedding** at St Michael's back a year to save money.
feel: **Alarmed**, with the ground going from under them as they start out.
S2.quote: The ground's going from under us just as we're starting out.
fieldNote: Zane would lean on his **future father-in-law**, not the state.
Delaying the **wedding** is his main lever, though he won't give it up.
He sees the **robot gap** as borrowed time rather than a chance to retrain.

steps.text: Ask Hannah's dad for full-time work on his cattle farm
Push the wedding at St Michael's back a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people should use it to get a proper trade. Apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd say that at church and to my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Till about 2034 for the lorry. I'd be thirty-four, married, maybe with a baby. I'd need a plan by then, but I'm not good at change. My dad's garage might be all I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my dad if I can do a proper apprenticeship with him over a couple of years, evenings and Saturdays. I'd keep driving the feed lorry. Hannah and I would get married as planned but keep it small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with something to aim at. The garage feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think garages are safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever. But old tractors and farm machinery need fixing by someone who knows them, and robots won't come to a muddy yard first. That's my bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mates who drive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands that's not just driving. And don't wait for the government to sort it.

say: I'd say people should use five years to get a **proper trade**.
I'd back **apprenticeships**, not handouts, at church and with mates.
think: The lorry lasts till about **2034**, when I may have a baby.
I'm not good at change, and **Dad's garage** might be all I've got.
do: Start a **mechanic apprenticeship** with his dad, evenings and Saturdays.
Marry as planned but keep the **wedding small**.
feel: **Worried** but with something to aim at in the **garage**.
S3.quote: Old tractors and farm machinery need fixing by someone who knows them, and robots won't come to a muddy yard first.
fieldNote: Five years gives Zane time for a **family apprenticeship**.
He still expects to lose **driving income** by 2034.
His trust is in **family and trade skills**, never government.

steps.text: Start an evening mechanic apprenticeship at his dad's garage
Keep the wedding small and on the planned date
Keep driving the bulk feed lorry meanwhile

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and people should just get on with it. Work hard and learn a trade. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work around 2039 means I'd have a lot of driving left. The office goes around 2036 but the lorry keeps rolling. I'd still be worried about the mill cutting back, but that's not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd change nothing. Get married, keep driving, maybe help Dad more at the garage. I'd think about it properly in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not too worried. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still worry about the mill. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the new owners don't care about this village. A big national group would close the feed mill if it made sense on a spreadsheet, robots or not. That's the real threat round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change when you and Hannah start a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably start sooner, while I've got a steady job. Hannah wants kids by thirty. That's the plan, God willing.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **get on with it**.
People should **work hard** and learn a trade.
think: Robots around **2039** leave a lot of driving left.
The **mill's owners** are the real threat, not AI.
do: Get **married** and keep driving the feed lorry.
Help his dad more at the **garage**.
Plan to start a **family** sooner while work is steady.
feel: **Not too worried**, because it feels far away.
S4.quote: A big national group would close the feed mill if it made sense on a spreadsheet, robots or not.
fieldNote: Zane says he's **not worried**, but the mill's takeover still threatens his hours.
Ten years mostly shapes his **family timing**.
He'd only plan properly **in a few years**.

steps.text: Keep driving the feed lorry and marry next June
Start a family sooner while the job is steady
Help his dad at the garage more often

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is proper apprenticeships for drivers in local trades, paid for by the firms that bring the robots in. Not benefits, just a fair chance to learn and earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about villages. When the feed mill goes, the pub goes, the shop goes. It's not just jobs, it's whether there's a village left.

headlineQuote: When the feed mill goes, the pub goes, the shop goes. It's not just jobs, it's whether there's a village left.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** bulk feed lorry driver serving farms around his village.
He's engaged to Hannah, with a **church wedding** next June and three weeks of savings.
He distrusts **big tech** and government and avoids AI completely.
He leans on **family**: his dad's garage and Hannah's father's farm.
He worries about the **mill takeover** as much as about robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be newly married with no income.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** in local trades, paid for by firms that bring in robots.
